headline: Stefanik family’s D.C. home sells to mystery buyer for $900K over list price
author: Joe Heim, Jon Swaine, Aaron Schaffer

paragraphs.text: Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-New York) was struggling to find a buyer.
The Capitol Hill rowhouse she had bought years earlier with her parents and brother was listed for sale in September 2025 for $2.195 million.
Just six blocks from the U.S. Capitol, the three-bedroom home on Independence Avenue SE was ideally located for someone hoping to live in the nation’s power corridor. The house, however, sat unsold.
Two months later, in November, the list price was cut to $1.99 million. In February of this year, five months after it was initially listed for sale, the home was taken off the market altogether.

But in June the property — still off the market — sold in an all-cash transaction for $2.9 million, or $910,000 more than its most recent list price, according to property records examined by The Washington Post. Only two homes on Capitol Hill are publicly listed as having sold for more in the past year.

The buyer was AFS Real Estate Holdings, a limited liability company formed in Delaware about a month before the sale. The company has no online presence, and a search of public records revealed no information about who owns it.

In a statement to The Post, Stefanik’s office said the home was publicly listed for sale during a government shutdown and “a slow holiday season” and was later sold in a “commercially reasonable transaction.” Her office said that she was a minority owner of the property and that off-market sales are increasingly common in Washington.
“The offer to buy the investment property was made and accepted within the range of prices for comparable historic townhouse sales in the neighborhood that range from $2-$4 million,” her office said.
Stefanik, who leaves office when her term expires in January, did not answer written questions asking if she knows who owns and operates AFS.

A half-dozen real estate agents and estate lawyers, none involved with the Stefanik property and each with decades of experience in the Capitol Hill neighborhood, told The Post they could recall no other transactions where a buyer paid so much more than what a seller had only recently been asking. Nor could they see why the Independence Avenue SE home would be so expensive.

“There may be outlying factors I’m not aware of, but from what I can see on the listing and the property records, it seems to be a very unusual purchase price,” said Patrick Tangney, a settlement attorney with two decades of experience with residential and commercial properties in the Washington region.

The Post found no records or work permits indicating that changes had been made to the home in the four-month period between when it was taken off the market and when it was sold. Records do not indicate there was any mortgage on the property at the time of the sale.

Stefanik, 42, announced in December that she would not seek reelection. Before this year she was chair of the House Republican Conference, a position to which she was elected by fellow GOP members and one that made her the fourth-highest-ranking Republican in the House. She was briefly seen as a possible vice-presidential candidate for Donald Trump in his 2024 White House bid.

The Independence Avenue SE home was recorded on June 24 as having been sold by EMS DC Properties, the limited liability company in which Stefanik and her family members were shareholders. EMS then purchased a newly built house in McLean, Virginia, for $3.3 million. Stefanik signed a document recording a $434,425 mortgage on that property. The document identifies her as “managing member” of EMS.

Janis M. Penman, the lawyer who filed papers to form AFS Real Estate Holdings, did not respond to a request for comment. Penman is a partner in the Washington office of the Cleveland-based firm BakerHostetler.

In response to questions from The Post, Stefanik’s office provided a list of 34 properties in the Capitol Hill neighborhood, “many” of which it said were comparable to hers. Records confirm that 13 of those properties fetched prices that were higher than Stefanik’s and the others sold for roughly similar amounts.

All but three, however, had more bedrooms than the Independence Avenue SE property and all but two had more living space. One of the properties with a similar sale price had a swimming pool and almost twice the square footage. Others were in particularly desirable locations, such as directly across from the Supreme Court. All but five had either a garage or one or more parking spaces.

To be considered comparable, real estate agents said, properties should have broadly similar features and sales ought to have been completed within months of each other. A majority of the properties on the list from Stefanik’s office were sold more than a year before hers.

At The Post’s request, Tom Faison, a real estate broker with more than three decades of experience on Capitol Hill, identified comparable properties through the Multiple Listing Service, or MLS, a database used by real estate brokers and agents.
“A reasonable appraiser looking at six months of sales in my opinion would not be able to justify $2.9 million for this house,” he said of the property on Independence Avenue SE.

Faison said that the home’s recent history on the market, and the fact that it did not sell at a lower price, revealed more about its value than any analysis of comparable properties. “I’ve never known a $3 million buyer, or any buyer, who would overlook the history,” he said.

Real estate listings describe the house as having 3.5 baths, three fireplaces and 2,700 square feet. It was not listed as having a garage or private parking spot, often a must for high-end buyers on Capitol Hill.

Developers and those who purchase rental properties sometimes do so through limited liability corporations, in part because such arrangements can simplify ownership among multiple partners. D.C. law requires the disclosure of owners of LLCs formed in the District but not of those formed elsewhere.

Stefanik, after graduating from Harvard in 2006, moved to Washington during the George W. Bush administration. She eventually took a job working for Joshua Bolten, then Bush’s White House chief of staff.

EMS DC Properties — “M” is both Stefanik’s middle initial and the initial of her brother’s first name — purchased the home on Independence Avenue SE in August 2010 for a little over $1.2 million. The property description for the listing that year touted the home as a one-of-a-kind renovation that “will knock your socks off.” It highlighted features including a “huge” chef’s kitchen, designer baths, a finished basement with bar and a rear deck and patio.

Stefanik’s father, Kenneth, signed a loan agreement for the house as a member of the company. Her mother, Melanie, later signed New York corporate registration paperwork as EMS’s chief financial officer, and her brother, Matthew Stefanik, signed loan documents as a company member.
Efforts to contact Stefanik’s parents and brother were not successful.

At the time of the purchase, Elise Stefanik was working for the leadership PAC of Tim Pawlenty, then the governor of Minnesota, who went on to explore a run for the Republican presidential nomination. Federal campaign records of Stefanik’s salary and expenses gave her address as the Independence Avenue SE house. Politico reported in September 2011 that Stefanik hosted a Pawlenty fundraiser at what it called “her Hill townhouse.”

In April 2013, Stefanik changed her voter registration from her parents’ home in Upstate New York to a lakeside house owned by her mother in that state’s 21st Congressional District. She ran for the seat the following year.

In a required financial disclosure filing during her 2014 campaign, Stefanik reported owning “residential rental property” in Washington via EMS DC Properties. Records do not show EMS owning any other properties in the capital. Stefanik valued her holding at between $250,001 and $500,000 and reported that it brought in rent of between $15,001 and $50,000.

Stefanik drew heat in the 2014 Republican primary from critics who accused her of living in a $1.2 million home purchased by her parents. Stefanik’s campaign responded that she was a New York resident and that she “owns 20 percent of a rental property in Washington, DC.”
Stefanik won her race and, at 30, was at the time the youngest woman ever elected to Congress.

Originally billing herself as a moderate Republican, Stefanik became a staunch ally of Trump during his first term. In 2025, on his first day back in office, Trump nominated her to be U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. He later withdrew the nomination to preserve the GOP’s slim majority in the House.

Stefanik had hoped for Trump’s endorsement in the Republican primary race for New York governor, but it never came. In December 2025, she dropped out of the contest and announced that she wouldn’t run again for her House seat.

By then her house was already on the market. In a Wall Street Journal story about the listing in September 2025, Stefanik described growing tomatoes in the yard, hosting family cookouts and cooking “Sunday sauce” in the kitchen of the open-layout first floor. She also said she liked to buy groceries from the butcher and cheese stand at Eastern Market, just steps from her home.
“One thing people may not know about me is I love to cook,” Stefanik told the Journal. “I come from a family of cooks.”

Earlier this year she published her first book, “Poisoned Ivies: The Inside Account of the Academic and Moral Rot at America’s Elite Universities,” an examination of top-tier universities becoming what she describes as “hotbeds of radical ideology, groundless elitism, intellectual laziness and anti-American hatred.”
Stefanik said in April that she had not ruled out running for any political office.
